what: A reranker takes the top results from a fast first search and reorders them with a smarter, slower model that reads the query and each document together. Only the best few go on to the user or the LLM.
like: Like a recruiter who skims 100 CVs by keyword, then a hiring manager who reads the top ones properly and picks the best 10.
why: Big jump in precision at the top (nDCG@10, MRR) for little extra code
Keeps the cheap first stage cheap - only ~100 candidates pay the expensive model
Better context for RAG: fewer, more relevant chunks mean better, cheaper LLM answers

steps.d: BM25 and a bi-encoder (query and documents embedded separately, ahead of time) pull candidates from millions of documents in milliseconds. The goal here is recall: get the right answer somewhere in the top 100.
Only a small window of candidates, with their text, moves on. Anything outside the window is never rescored, so first-stage recall@100 sets the ceiling.
The model reads query and document together in one pass, so every query word can attend to every document word. Much more accurate, but it must run once per pair.
ColBERT stores one vector per document token. At query time each query token finds its best match (MaxSim) and the maxima are summed. Close to cross-encoder quality, far cheaper.
An LLM can order passages listwise. RankGPT slides a window of 20 from the bottom up in steps of 10. Strong, but the slowest and most costly option.
The reordered top 10 goes to the user or into the LLM prompt. AI answer engines retrieve, rerank and then cite only the few pages that survive.

choices.d: How many candidates to rerank. Bigger raises the chance the right one is in the pool but costs more time; 50-100 is common. Measure recall@K of the first stage to pick it.

Hosted: Cohere Rerank, Voyage rerank, Elastic Rerank via the text_similarity_reranker retriever. Self-hosted: bge-reranker or other cross-encoders. Late interaction (ColBERT) if you can store per-token vectors.
Rerankers read limited text. Rerank passages, not whole sites; long documents get truncated or split, and the best chunk score usually stands for the document.
Reranking runs on every search, so it adds directly to response time. Batch pairs on a GPU, use a lite model for live traffic, or cache results for popular queries.
Instead of always passing 10 chunks to the LLM, drop anything below a relevance score. Fewer, better chunks cut tokens and reduce wrong citations.

instead.why: Fusion alone with RRF: no model cost, smaller quality lift
The cheap first stage the reranker sits on top of
An LLM as listwise reranker: strongest reasoning, slowest and priciest
Prove the reranker helps: nDCG@10 and MRR on a labelled set

breaks.d: The reranker can only reorder what the first stage found.
breaks.see: Low recall@100 on the eval set even though nDCG@10 of found items is fine
breaks.fix: Improve the first stage: hybrid BM25 + vectors, better chunking, a bigger window

breaks.d: Reranking 200 long passages per query on CPU blows the time budget.
breaks.see: p95 search latency (the slowest 1 in 20 requests) jumps after launch
breaks.fix: Smaller window, shorter passages, GPU batching, a lite model or late interaction

breaks.d: Text past the model's limit is cut, so the key paragraph is never read.
breaks.see: Relevant long pages rank low; the matching text sits deep in the page
breaks.fix: Chunk before reranking and score the best chunk per document

breaks.d: A general reranker misjudges your jargon or product names.
breaks.see: nDCG@10 on your own queries is lower than the vendor benchmark
breaks.fix: Add instructions where supported, fine-tune on your click or label data, or blend with BM25

say: I'll use two stages: BM25 plus vector search fused with RRF to get a high-recall top 100, then a cross-encoder reranker for precision on the top 10.
The bi-encoder is fast because document vectors are precomputed; the cross-encoder is accurate because it reads query and document together, so I only run it on the shortlist.
I'll measure recall@100 for the first stage and nDCG@10 and MRR after reranking, so I know which stage to fix.
If latency is tight, I'll try ColBERT-style late interaction or a lite reranker, and cache results for the most popular queries.

followups.q: Why not run the cross-encoder over the whole corpus?
followups.a: It must process every query-document pair at query time, with no precomputed vectors. Over millions of documents that is far too slow, so it only reorders a shortlist from a fast retriever.

ColBERT encodes query and document separately into one vector per token. Scoring sums, for each query token, its maximum similarity to any document token (MaxSim). Document vectors are precomputed, so it is much cheaper than a cross-encoder.

followups.q: How do nDCG@10 and MRR differ?
followups.a: MRR looks at the rank of the first relevant result only: 1 for top spot, 1/2 for second. nDCG@10 uses graded relevance for all top 10 results and rewards putting the most relevant ones highest.

followups.q: How does this relate to AI answer engines citing pages?
followups.a: They retrieve many candidates, rerank, and pass only the top few passages to the LLM, which cites them. A page that is clear, specific and matches the question well survives reranking and gets cited.

today: Rerank models now read long inputs: Cohere's rerank-v5.0 accepts up to 32,768 tokens shared between query and document and up to 10,000 documents per request, so whole pages can often be scored without manual chunking.

check.q: Why do we rerank only the top ~100 and not every document?
check.a: The cross-encoder must score each query-document pair, which is slow
check.why: Cross-encoders cannot precompute document vectors, so cost grows with every pair scored.

check.q: What makes a bi-encoder fast for first-stage retrieval?
check.a: Document embeddings are computed ahead of time and searched with an index
d: It reads query and document together
It uses an LLM to rank results
check.why: Only the query is embedded at search time; the rest is a nearest-neighbour lookup.

check.q: In ColBERT, what does MaxSim do?
check.a: For each query token, takes its best-matching document token similarity
d: Averages all document vectors into one
check.why: The per-token maxima are summed to give the document's score.

check.q: nDCG@10 went up after adding a reranker, but recall@100 is unchanged. What does that tell you?
check.a: The reranker improved the order, not what was found
check.why: A reranker only reorders candidates. Recall is set by the first stage.
